opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the crowdsourced benchmark we leaned on most was BIG-bench, which was a collaborative effort where researchers from many different institutions contributed tasks, eventually more than two hundred of them. What made it so valuable was that the tasks weren't designed by any one group with a particular notion of what "reasoning" should look like. You had logical deduction, analogies, cause-and-effect questions, explaining jokes, multi-step arithmetic, and some genuinely quirky tasks that I don't think any of us would have thought to write ourselves.

The first lesson was that aggregate numbers hide a lot. Overall, PaLM did quite well. On a meaningful subset of tasks it outperformed the average human rater who attempted them. But when you broke results down task by task, the picture was much more varied. Some tasks improved smoothly and predictably as we scaled from the 8 billion to the 62 billion to the 540 billion parameter model. Others stayed flat for a long time and then jumped sharply at the largest scale. We called those discontinuous improvements. And on some tasks the model barely moved at all. If we'd had only a handful of benchmarks, we could easily have concluded that scaling helps everything uniformly, or that it doesn't help reasoning at all, depending on which benchmarks we happened to pick.

The second lesson was about humility in how we define capabilities. Because the tasks came from such a diverse community, they probed things in ways that exposed both surprising strengths and blind spots. That breadth is really the only way to get an honest picture of what a model can and can't do, as opposed to a picture shaped by the assumptions of the people building it.

The third piece, which ties into the chain-of-thought work we were doing at the same time, was that some tasks looked hard purely because of how they were posed. When we prompted the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps, performance on certain multi-step tasks changed dramatically. Having many benchmarks let us see which tasks were sensitive to prompting and which reflected deeper limitations.

So my takeaway is that no single benchmark, or even a small suite, captures what we mean by intelligence or reasoning. You want a broad, diverse, ideally community-built set of evaluations, because that's what reveals the shape of a model's capabilities rather than just a single number.

r001.rationale: The response says a broad, diverse benchmark set exposed surprising strengths and blind spots, and that a small set could have missed the varied capabilities PaLM showed.

r002.rationale: The response describes benchmarks revealing tasks where PaLM struggled, but does not say those questions guide progress toward the next generation of models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was BIG-bench, which is the Beyond the Imitation Game benchmark, and it was this really interesting collaborative effort where more than a hundred different institutions contributed tasks. I think it ended up being over two hundred tasks when we ran it. And what's special about it is that each task was contributed by someone who had a particular hypothesis about what language models can't do. So you have things like logical deduction, you have tasks where you have to figure out the punchline of a joke, tasks about causal judgment, tasks that involve multi-step arithmetic, even things like navigating a sequence of directions and figuring out where you end up.

And the thing we learned, honestly, is that if you only look at one or two benchmarks, you get a very distorted picture of what a model can do. When we evaluated PaLM on BIG-bench, the aggregate number looked good, and in fact it was better than the average human rater on the tasks we looked at. But that aggregate hides enormous variance. There were tasks where scaling from 8 billion to 62 billion to 540 billion parameters gave you this smooth, predictable improvement. There were other tasks where nothing happened at the smaller scales and then suddenly at 540 billion the model just got it, which is the discontinuous or emergent behavior people have talked about. And then there were tasks where the model was flat, or barely above chance, regardless of scale. Things like certain kinds of mathematical induction, or tasks that require tracking a lot of state.

So the value of having many benchmarks is really about diagnosis. A single benchmark tells you whether you're better or worse than the last model. Hundreds of diverse tasks tell you where you're better, and which capabilities are actually unlocking versus which ones are stuck. That's the information you need as a researcher to decide what to work on next. If I only had, say, a reading comprehension benchmark, I would have had no idea that the model was struggling with certain forms of logical reasoning while being surprisingly good at explaining jokes.

The other lesson was about contamination and saturation. Older benchmarks tend to get saturated fairly quickly, and some of them leak into the training data, so the number stops meaning what you think it means. Having a large, fresh, crowdsourced set helps with that, because no single team's blind spots define what "good" looks like. Different people bring different ideas about what hard means, and that diversity is what makes the evaluation honest.

r001.rationale: The response says diverse tasks revealed PaLM’s uneven abilities, including logical reasoning struggles and unexpected strengths that a narrow benchmark would miss.

r002.rationale: It explains that crowdsourced tasks tested suspected model weaknesses and that the resulting diagnosis helps researchers decide what to work on next.

astra-6.text:
One thing it highlighted is that reasoning isn’t a single capability. A model can do well on one kind of problem and still struggle with another. With a crowdsourced benchmark, you get a much broader range of tasks and perspectives than any one research team would think to include.

So having many different benchmarks helps us understand where the model’s capabilities are emerging and where the gaps remain. It also keeps us from taking success on one benchmark as evidence that we’ve solved reasoning more generally.

r001.rationale: It says a crowdsourced benchmark covers a broader range of tasks than one team might include, helping reveal where model capabilities are emerging.

r002.rationale: It mentions identifying gaps, but does not say that sourcing questions to expose current models’ difficulties guides the next generation of models.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing we learned from evaluating PaLM on BIG-bench, which brings together tasks contributed by many different people, was how much a single benchmark can hide. You might see steady improvement on an aggregate score, but when you look at individual tasks, the behavior can be very different. Some improve gradually with scale, while others show a much more dramatic jump at the largest model size.

That diversity is valuable because people come up with ways to test reasoning that we, as model developers, might not have thought of. It helps us discover capabilities, but also understand where the model still struggles. So having many different benchmarks gives us a much richer picture than asking whether the model does well on one particular test.

r001.rationale: It says diverse contributor-designed tests can reveal reasoning capabilities developers might not have thought to test for.

r002.rationale: It says varied tests help reveal where the model struggles, but does not connect sourcing questions that expose difficulties to guiding progress toward the next generation of models.
